articles.title: Northern Ireland tourism: Mixed picture for businesses
articles.summary: Tourism NI says that "the vast majority of tourism businesses are largely optimistic" but what do businesses say?
articles.body:
It's been a summer of hot weather and big events, perfect conditions, you'd think, for a bumper tourism season.

But according to industry leaders the picture across Northern Ireland has been more mixed.

According to Tourism NI "the vast majority of tourism businesses are largely optimistic".

Representatives of the hospitality sector say that margins are tight and that, although the number of hotel beds sold is well up, occupancy levels were flat as there are more hotels.

All seem to agree, however, that large events are a means of growing the industry.

Tourism NI says its research "found that the vast majority of tourism businesses are largely optimistic".

Figures released this week by NISRA record that July set a new record for hotel bed and room bookings with nearly 40,000 more rooms sold than the same month a year ago.

But Janice Gault of the NI Hotels Federation says hotels still face challenges.

"I think the summer was very reflective of the weather," she says. "Periods of real heat, periods of coolness and a lot of uncertainty.

"Occupancy was probably slightly down but we now have more hotel rooms so we sold more rooms across a wider portfolio. Events are the big thing. They are the thing that completely change the picture."

The All-Ireland Fleadh's first visit to Belfast was the poster child for this, delivering an estimated 1.65m visits and estimated spend of more than £53m .

Colin Neill from Hospitality Ulster agrees.

He says attracting big events and enticing visitors back must be the ambition.

"Events and experiences are what drive people," he says. "It's what brings tourism from outside and inside the province. The Tourist Board need more money to market in the Republic of Ireland because we need to attract those Fleadh people out around other towns on their next visit."

Away from the Fleadh, many smaller festivals also recorded healthy numbers. In Warrenpoint, for example, estimated numbers at the annual Wake the Giant festival rose by 5,000 to nearly 25,000.

And with school bells ringing again and evenings cutting off, this weekend perhaps marks the end of that traditional festival season.

Two large events taking place are Eats & Beats in Newcastle and Armagh's Food & Cider Weekend.

Setting up the festival village in Newcastle is Lynn Campbell.

She says the music and food event is about more than what is experienced on the day.

"This is the last wee boost for summer that will bring a big crowd into Newcastle," she adds.

"But the hope is that people who come here to the festival will then venture up the town and see what it has to offer – not just in summer but to come back throughout the year."

This year is the first time the annual event has been ticketed – that's because in recent times more people have attended than Donard Park can cater for.

"At any one time 6,000 can fit in the festival site," Lynn says. "That will fluctuate but across the weekend we are hoping for up to 15,000 visitors."

In Armagh they are also gearing up for the Orchard County's annual celebration of it's most famous product – the apple.

"We have murder mystery dinners here on Friday and Saturday night and then a tour on Sunday afternoon," says Philip Troughton of The Armagh Cider Company.

"It's obviously excellent for us as it raises the profile of the product, the apples and what's a very young industry here in County Armagh."

But it's an industry Philip feels needs less regulation if it is to achieve its potential.

"The licencing laws, at present, forbid me to sell cider on site. We have diversified into tourism and we take in groups and show them the facilities and the orchards and they can taste the ciders but if you look at any vineyard in France, you can try their product and you can buy their products.

"There has been a slackening but they are still very restrictive."

And it is this suggestion that taxation and regulation is stifling tourism growth that regularly comes up in discussion and debate.

This week the level of hospitality tax in NI compared to the Republic and its impact was discussed at Westminster .

Back in Belfast restaurateur Simon McCance says that 40% of his turnover is in some way tax related.

"There's 20% on VAT, our rates bills are big, then there's NI Contributions and other things like waste disposal, water and minimum wage increases," he says.

He says tourism has been steady but there are external pressures.

"August is usually a good month for us with tourism and you do see people from all over the world coming here but I would think that we haven't seen as many Americans coming here as we have in the past, which I'm pretty sure is due to the cost of living."

Among the firms to avail of the scheme was Life Adventure Centre in Castlewellan.

According to Martin McMullan it proved beneficial.

"We were able to keep prices down and offer some special offers through the summer," he says adding that he would like to see it in place permanently.

"We saw was a good mix of national and international visitors. We are seeing more and more of them coming to places like this rather than just to Belfast for the day."

But perhaps the final thought on summer 2026 should go to the ice cream industry.

Michael Nugent of Nugelato has 13 ice cream outlets across Northern Ireland, including some in seaside locations.

He says the good summer weather was reflected in different consumer patterns compared to previous years, especially in his Newcastle shop.

"Because the weather was so good we were steadily busy rather than being busy in mad bursts as you would be in a normal summer," he says.

"People didn't have to rush to the seaside because they thought it was their only chance. So trade was up but it was a more steady flow."

However, Nugent says it balanced out a very "wet" start to the year.

"The cost of doing business only goes up so you are also trying to absorb that too," he adds.

articles.title: Lime apologises to blind couple over bike-blocked pavement
articles.summary: Jason Beal says he was forced onto a busy road when Lime bikes were blocking pavements in a banned area.
articles.body:
E-bike company Lime has apologised to a blind couple after an app glitch led to bikes being left to block pavements in south-east London.

Jessica and Jason Beal, who live in Penge, said an influx of e-bikes left on footpaths created dangerous hazards.

Describing a recent encounter on his route, Jason said an abandoned bike forced him to go into the busy main road with his guide dog.

Bromley Council does not permit Lime to operate in the borough. However, a now-fixed issue with Lime's app mistakenly enabled users to start and end rentals in Penge, which borders the neighbouring borough of Lewisham where the service is authorised.

Jessica said: "We really think bikes is a great way to get around, especially in London.

"It's just to for people to be much more mindful of where they're leaving them and the speed they're riding them."

Lime confirmed it had updated its geofencing technology to block rentals and parking across the Penge boundary.

A spokesperson for Lime said they were sorry about the issues caused for the couple.

"We acted fast to remove any bikes in Penge when alerted, and have tightened our geofencing to avoid this becoming a regular occurrence."

Bromley Council welcomed the correction to the app but warned it would take tough action if the problem recurred.

Simon Fawthrop, executive member for transport and highways, said the council had long-held misgivings about bikes that are "strewn across pavements causing multiple hazards".

He warned the council would take action to remove the Lime bikes and then charge Lime for the cost.

Mike Wordingham, from the Royal National Institute of Blind People (RNIB), said the incident highlighted a broader issue for disabled pedestrians in London.

He said research by the sight loss charity found 81% of blind and partially-sighted respondents said bikes and e-scooters left on pavements made their journeys harder, and 11% said the issue stopped them going out altogether.

Liam Conlon, the MP for Beckenham and Penge, said there needed to be proper contracts in place to ensure e-bike firms behaved in a responsible way.

He called for more designated parking zones and time limits for firms to remove e-bikes and scooters causing a nuisance.

articles.title: Dedicated officer to combat homes pumping sewage into waterways
articles.summary: Misconnections happen when incorrectly installed plumbing allows waste water to be diverted to surface drains.
articles.body:
A dedicated officer is to be hired in west London in a trial to combat the problem of water-polluting misconnections.

Owing to incorrect plumbing, affected households pump waste into surface drains, which can then spread, killing wildlife and damaging waterways.

Local authorities can take enforcement action, and if the pilot - funded by the mayor of London's office - is successful, the measure could be rolled out across the capital.

Funding is to be spent where the issue is considered a particular problem, including the River Brent catchment area.

Founder of the volunteer group Clean Up the River Brent (CURB), Ben Morris, said there was "good reason" to think misconnections "are the biggest single cause of pollution in London's rivers".

He added: "We need to see stronger action from the councils to get this done.

"They have the power of enforcement and they need to be using those powers to get those property owners to sort out the misconnections."

An information request to Thames Water by the charity Friends of the River Crane Environment (FORCE ) revealed that in October 2024 seven blocks of flats in north and west London were identified as having misconnections.

FORCE said this meant at least 100 homes were flushing waste into the rivers Crane and Brent.

Since then, only three of the seven blocks' misconnections have been resolved, according to Thames Water.

The company said two of the housing developments still pumping out sewage were in the borough of Barnet, while two were in the borough of Harrow.

It said the other three, which were in Ealing borough, have since had their misconnections fixed.

It did not provide details of where exactly the properties are.

Barnet Council said it was committed to resolving misconnections "as quickly and effectively as possible".

Harrow Council's press office did not respond to the BBC's request for a response.

Mete Coban, deputy mayor of London for environment, said the project would "beef up" councils by giving them resources needed to properly enforce action against misconnections.

"City Hall has funded a dedicated officer to operate within the council, to get to the root cause of misconnections, working with the landlords and others to make sure that we're actually dealing with this issue."

The project is part of a 10-year plan to clean up some of London's rivers and waterways, announced by Sir Sadiq Khan in July.

Among ten locations earmarked for funding are the Grand Union Canal, the River Brent catchment area, and the Lower Crane Valley.

A total of £1.8bn has been pledged by water companies, boroughs and charities, with London's mayor adding £2.7m across three years, on top of £13.6m already promised.

A Thames Water spokesperson said households and buildings which have connected wastewater appliances to the wrong drainage system can have a serious impact on the environment.

"While we are not responsible for third-party drainage, we work closely with partners to tackle this significant issue across our catchment. Of the seven cases identified across North and West London, three have now been resolved, while work continues on the remaining cases.

"Most misconnections are done entirely by accident, but the responsibility remains with the property owner, which is why we would urge freeholders or developers fitting new connections to make sure they're plumbed in properly."

A Barnet Council spokesperson said the investigations "can be complex, involving multiple people and organisations" but they were "committed to resolving them as quickly and effectively as possible".

articles.title: Freddie Mercury mural unveiled at Wembley for 80th birthday
articles.summary: The artwork is anamorphic, so the image only resolves when viewed from a single marked spot about 65ft away.
articles.body:
A 30ft (9m) mural of Freddie Mercury has been unveiled at Wembley Park to mark what would have been the singer's 80th birthday.

The artwork, called I'm Mr Mercury, is anamorphic, meaning the image only resolves when viewed from a single marked spot about 65ft away. From anywhere else it breaks up into colour and line.

It was created by the street artist Frank Styles, who hand-sprayed it as four separate works before composing them into a single image across all 58 of the site's Spanish Steps.

Mercury, born on 5 September 1946, performed at Wembley repeatedly with Queen.

The band played 10 shows at the venue, previously known as the Empire Pool, between 1978 and 1984, and appeared at Live Aid at Wembley Stadium in July 1985. Queen returned to the stadium for two sold-out concerts the following summer.

The mural also refers to Mercury's life away from the stage. Koi carp reflect his love of Japan and the Japanese pond at his London home, while winged female figures echo his Virgo star sign, a motif he used on the Queen crest he designed himself.

Lyrics and quotations run up the steps towards the stadium.

Claudio Giambrone, who commissioned and curated the work for Wembley Park, said: "Freddie Mercury's relationship with Wembley goes far beyond a single famous performance.

"We wanted to create something that gives fans a new place in Wembley where they can come together and remember him."

Styles said: "As a trained graphic designer himself, Freddie was very aware and precise about the visual feel and so I have endeavoured to follow his ethos in the conscious creation of this mural."

The steps link Wembley Stadium and the OVO Arena, formerly Wembley Arena. The mural is free to view at any time and will remain in place until December 2026.

articles.title: Guernsey Police warns of risks when posting school photos
articles.summary: Parents are being urged to think about any identifying information that may be in photos online.
articles.body:
Guernsey Police has warned parents about posting back-to-school photos containing identifying information on social media.

This followed a social media post by Sussex Police that highlighted how the photos could allow individuals to create Artificial-Intelligence (AI) generated child abuse imagery or identify a family's location and schedule.

Not-for-profit organisations and supervisory data bodies have encouraged parents to be aware when posting such photos when schools return for the next term.

Det Insp Tom Lowe, from Guernsey Police, said: "We're not trying to discourage people recording these memories [but wish to] highlight the risk."

Lowe said AI allows "more opportunity for people to exploit images being posted online".

He said the police aimed to "raise awareness" so parents could "make the judgement correctly" when posting photos online.

Lowe pointed to the social media post by Sussex Police as an example of how "a picture can contain a thousand little minutiae" that could allow people with "malicious intent" to pick up on identifying information.

"Think about house names, road names, vehicle identifiers and if your son or daughter is holding specific items containing their names," he said.

Guernsey Police wanted parents to be aware what information is "out in the public and can be utilised".

Lowe said the police continued to "work with Home Affairs to ensure that the laws needed are put forward and put into place" regarding AI technology.

Ghislaine Bombusa, from online safety organisation Internet Matters, said parents should "take a pause" and think "what is identifiable" when sharing back-to-school photos online.

She said parents should "celebrate moments with their children" but be aware of what images could be used for.

"This image of your child can be turned into a sexualised or an abusive image," she said.

Bombusa added the more information is shared, the more parents were "giving opportunities for people to build a picture of your child".

"This is where they live, this is where I can find them, this is where they go to school, that is a potential risk," she added.

She made clear that the organisation was not "saying you can't share at all" but making sure parents are "taking that pause and time to check" before sharing images and information.

Rachel Masteron, deputy data protection officer at the Office for Data Protection Authority in Guernsey, said the information in school photos could allow individuals to "identify locations and possibly work out passwords".

Masterton pointed out how "even a parents name on a coffee cup" in a photo could allow "somebody who might want to do nefarious things" to win a child's trust.

She said: "As a child you are more likely to think, they do know me so maybe I will go with them."

Masterton said it was a "sad indictment of the world today that we need to be thinking like this but it is there".

The shared information could reveal families were on holiday "therefore your home is ready for someone to break into" or posting pictures of a child could mean "their images might be taken and used in a deep fake", she said.

Masterton said authorities do not want parents to "overthink to the point of paralysis" when posting online but having all the information posted online "in one place could be where it starts to cause bigger problems".

"It allows information to be linked together and used in ways that you might not expect," she said.

articles.title: New Somerset club night hopes to promote young local DJs
articles.summary: The event wants to bring big names to smaller-town venues that typically struggle to attract them.
articles.body:
A new club night is looking to establish a stage for local up-and-coming DJs to play alongside big names, bringing together promoters and artists to help grow the Drum and Bass (DnB) scene in Somerset.

XYZ Events are an independent events company from Somerset who want to give people the opportunity to discover underground music locally, without having to travel to bigger cities.

Their debut event, in Wells, will see renowned DnB artists such as Ed Solo and Brockie share the stage with Somerset-based acts such DJ CLOVA, from Bath, and 3SEVEN6, from Glastonbury.

"It's very exciting to see [the scene] branching out. It's really nice to see it spreading out to other towns," said DJ CLOVA, 25.

Meadows restored by charity man set up as dying wish

Nightclubs and underground music venues have been declining across the UK since the pandemic.

The Night Time Industries Association say about 800 venues have closed nationally since March 2020.

DJ CLOVA, whose real name is Chloe Athay, says people her age typically have to go to Bristol to hear the music they love.

"Bristol is the heart of DnB in the United Kingdom, so that's the place to be - but it's a shame to not see so much in Bath, and to see an event in Wells is very exciting," she said.

Athay says there is a following for DnB and underground music in Somerset, adding there needs to be more space for it, as nightlife options are currently "limited" and people do not always want to travel far on a night out.

"I think it will open it up to more of the older generation, who might feel a stigma about going to the bigger cities - and there are loads of students.

"I think it will be really nice to see," she said.

The event marks a return for XYZ, who were putting on events in Somerset before the Covid lockdowns.

XYZ's founder, Keanan Kruse, 40, hopes that bringing big names to the area will help local venues.

"I think the main problem is transport in the rural areas," he said. "There's a lot of small and mid-size venues that are struggling to get the known artists to the area, so we're trying to bridge that gap."

The event is taking place in Studio24 in Wells, a former bingo hall that reopened as a live music venue in 2024, having previously been a nightclub.

Kruse said he hopes the event will "help get the venue popping and will have a good impact on the local economy".

"It's bringing a bit of a community together, including faces that I knew were in the scene but didn't know personally," he said.

articles.title: Two Reform officials step down after undercover report on party donations
articles.summary: Reform says Dan Jukes and James Orr have left their roles as it launches an investigation into the report.
articles.body:
Reform UK says two senior officials have stepped down as the party launched an investigation into claims about funding aired during a Channel 4 News report.

Nigel Farage's senior aide Dan Jukes and Reform's head of policy James Orr have both stood down pending the outcome of the internal probe, the party said.

The party added the investigation should be "allowed to proceed independently and without prejudice" and it would make no further comment for now.

The row threatens to overshadow Reform's conference in Birmingham, which has its first full day on Friday.

In the Channel 4 report, which aired on Thursday night, undercover filming showed Jukes suggesting a way to get around electoral law to secure a foreign donation of £500,000 for the party.

The undercover filming was carried out by a group called Verbatim Investigations, which was founded by journalists from the Centre for Climate Reporting. Channel 4 News say they have verified the material they were given and chose to broadcast.

Reform has denied any wrongdoing and said it had "been the target of a hoax perpetuated by foreign-funded climate change activists".

Labour and the Liberal Democrats have reported Reform to the Metropolitan Police over the allegations. The force said on Thursday it would assess the matter and any information provided to it.

In a statement on Friday, the Electoral Commission said: "We are considering all relevant information, in line with our regulatory remit, and we are in touch with the Met Police.

"The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500.

"Information about any potential attempt to evade the controls on donations is for the police to consider."

Jukes said he denied wrongdoing and had "stepped back from politics in order to clear my name." The BBC has contacted Orr for a comment.

Reacting on Friday, Farage told LBC a "couple of our contractors have said things that shouldn't have been said" and had been "removed this morning".

The Reform UK leader added: "The party has broken no laws, the party has not taken any dodgy money or anything like that whatsoever."

Farage appears to be trying to distance himself Jukes and Orr, with his comments to LBC.

However Jukes is widely seen as Farage's closest aide, who is often at his side, and is judged to have an innate sense of his boss's instincts. Jukes has long been the man you need to call if you want to arrange an interview with the Reform UK leader.

Orr, a Cambridge academic who has stepped down the party's head of policy, could also be considered to be in Farage's inner circle.

Channel 4 broadcast footage from a lunch in Clacton in Essex, with a reporter posing as the UK-based son, and an actor posing as his supposed American father. Opposite them are both Jukes and Farage.

Farage says "it's all above board" after the son has told him he has been in discussions with both Jukes and Reform's policy chief, James Orr about it for some time.

"I'll be the registered donor," the son says. "But then dad will send the money to me, and then as soon as that's done and all those conversations are had the money is available."

"Thank you. Well, both of you. Thank you," Farage is heard saying.

Farage senior aide filmed suggesting way to avoid donations law

Electoral law sets out that to be a permissible donor to a UK political party you must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK.

In this instance, the son would be a permissible donor, his father would not be.

Earlier in Channel 4 News's film, prior to the suggested £500,000 donation, Channel 4 says Orr suggests to the undercover reporter that perhaps his father could pay for opinion polling to aid Reform's campaigning.

The poll would cost £18,000 plus VAT – and Orr suggests that perhaps the polling company could send the bill to the undercover reporter.

In all, Channel 4 News says Reform commissioned three polls costing £32,500 in total and that the public was not told who commissioned or funded them.

Not disclosing such funding would be illegal and accepting this kind of foreign funding would also be illegal.

An Electoral Commission spokesperson said on Thursday: "The law requires political parties to report all permissible donations they accept with a value over £11,180 and all impermissible donations over £500.

On Friday morning, Reform UK chairman Lee Anderson told Sky News there was "no chance" of Jukes and Orr returning to the party.

This appeared to be contradicted by Reform's deputy leader Richard Tice, who told BBC Radio 4's Today programme minutes later that "it's not actually, in the nicest possible way, for any individual to make that determination" as the investigation continues.

articles.title: A retired North Carolina repairman built giant wind-powered sculptures from scrap; after 30 were moved downtown, the park drew 194,300 visitors and generated $5.3 million in regional sales
articles.summary: US News: Vollis Simpson spent much of his life repairing farm machinery in Wilson County, North Carolina. After retiring, he began building huge wind-powered s.
articles.body: Vollis Simpson spent much of his life repairing farm machinery in Wilson County, North Carolina. After retiring, he began building huge wind-powered sculptures on his farm using discarded materials. What started as a hobby soon grew into a collection that drew visitors from across the country.Simpson, a self-taught folk artist, began building the monumental kinetic sculptures in his 60s. According to the Vollis Simpson Whirligig Park & Museum, he used salvaged road signs, bicycle parts and scrap metal to create towering structures that moved with the wind. The works later became recognised as examples of American Folk Art.The sculptures first stood on Simpson’s farm in Lucama, about 11 miles outside Wilson. As word spread, especially after the rise of the internet, visitors began travelling to see them. The farm eventually became Wilson County’s top tourist destination, according to a 2020 economic impact report prepared for the City of Wilson.But Simpson grew older and the sculptures began to deteriorate. The Wilson community then worked to preserve his creations and bring them into the city. The result was the Vollis Simpson Whirligig Park, a roughly two-acre public art park in downtown Wilson that opened in November 2017.From farm collection to downtown parkThe park was created through a public-private partnership involving the City of Wilson and the nonprofit Vollis Simpson Whirligig Park and Museum. It now contains 30 restored large-scale kinetic sculptures.The move was a major undertaking, involving the conservation and installation of the sculptures at the new downtown site. The aim was not only to preserve Simpson’s work but also to create a public gathering space and encourage activity in downtown Wilson.That effort appears to have had a measurable economic effect. A 2020 economic impact study found that, during the park’s early years, visitors from outside the region generated about $1.7 million in spending in Wilson County annually. After accounting for the wider economic ripple effects, tourism linked to the park generated about $752,000 in annual earnings and supported 28 full-time jobs.Property values rose around the parkThe study also examined property values in an area containing about 340 parcels around the park. In 2009, before the park project was announced, properties in the study area had a combined assessed value of about $49.8 million. By 2019, that figure had reached $67.7 million, a 36% increase.The report compared that rise with property values across Wilson. The total assessed value within the city remained almost unchanged during the same period. The park area therefore had gained more than $17.9 million in assessed value over the 10-year period.Commercial activity also increased. Property owners and real estate professionals interviewed for the report described the park as a major asset and a “draw” for downtown.One property owner said they “would not have done” their first redevelopment project without the positive announcements around the Whirligig Park and nearby Whirligig Station.The report said the park and other downtown investments helped create what one interviewee called a “destination”, while another described the change as going from “dead to active”.Visitor numbers have grownThe park’s visitor numbers have continued to grow since the period covered by the 2020 study. According to the Whirligig Park’s current figures, about 194,300 people visited the park in 2024, including roughly 92,550 visitors from outside the region.The park says its annual economic impact has now reached $5.3 million in total regional sales, with an annual income impact of $1.9 million and 42 jobs supported.In 2019, regular visitation was estimated at about 90 people a day, or nearly 32,850 visitors for the year. The study also found that visitors from outside Wilson County were an important source of new spending because their money was considered new economic activity for the county.Simpson’s work lives onSimpson died in 2013, four years before the park opened. But the sculptures he built from scrap continue to form the centrepiece of downtown Wilson.The park now presents 30 of his restored works in one location, allowing visitors to see the machines that once stood on his farm. The organisation behind the park continues to operate it through its partnership with the City of Wilson.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 1988, diver Todd Barber watched a Cayman reef die, then invented hand-launched Reef Balls; his foundation’s modules now create habitat in over 70 countries
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Todd Barber was diving around Grand Cayman when Hurricane Gilbert damaged the coral reef he had known since childhood. The experience led Barber and h.
articles.body: Todd Barber was diving around Grand Cayman when Hurricane Gilbert damaged the coral reef he had known since childhood. The experience led Barber and his father, Jerry, to look for a way to create artificial reef structures that could be transported and deployed without the heavy equipment that is generally used for large underwater installations.Their answer was the Reef Ball, which is a hollow concrete module with openings that provide shelter for marine organisms. The Reef Ball Foundation's history says the Barbers developed and patented the design after seeing the condition of the Cayman reef.Barber founded the Reef Ball Development Group in 1993, and that August the group's first ocean test reef, which consisted of three Reef Balls, was deployed south of Peanut Island in Florida's Intracoastal Waterway.A concrete sphere designed to move without cranesThe modules were built around inflatable objects, initially beach balls and later a central inflatable bladder. The hollow structure could be floated to a site by a small boat and then sunk by deflating the interior once the concrete hardened, which made the system different from artificial reefs created by sinking ships, vehicles or other heavy objects.The Reef Ball Foundation says the Barbers worked with researchers and colleagues from the University of Georgia, the Nationwide Artificial Reef Coordinators and the Florida Institute of Technology while refining the design. The foundation says a pH-neutral, hardened microsilica concrete was selected, while rough surface treatments were used to encourage organisms such as corals, algae and sponges to settle on the modules.The first tests came in 1993The first Reef Ball ocean test was modest, wherein three modules were placed in the water in August 1993. A contemporary September 1993 report from Waterfront News described the Barbers as the inventors of the inflatable concrete structures and said that the modules were intended to be inexpensive enough for local dive clubs and other groups to build and deploy.The early design was built around a four-foot-diameter inflatable structure, and the concrete shell contained openings that created protected spaces for juvenile fish and other marine organisms. Reef Ball's first test reef was expanded with newer designs in 1994 and later dedicated as a memorial reef.By 1997, the Reef Ball Foundation had been established as a nonprofit organization, which expanded the work beyond the original artificial-reef concept.From one reef to an international systemThe foundation says Reef Balls became internationally established after 300 modules were deployed in Cancun, Mexico, in 1994. Projects later spread across the United States and into Europe, the Arabian Gulf, Canada, Brazil, the Caribbean, Indonesia and Africa. The foundation now says Reef Balls have been used in 59 or more countries, while its projects have a global reach of more than 70 countries, and also reports more than 6,500 projects and more than half a million Reef Balls deployed.Those figures cover a much broader organization than the original 1993 development group, since the foundation's work now includes coral rescue and propagation, oyster and kelp reefs, mangrove restoration, living shorelines and other habitat projects.The modules became habitatThe basic principle has remained the same, which was to place a stable structure on the seabed and give marine organisms surfaces and protected spaces on which to settle. The foundation says Reef Balls are designed to resemble natural reef formations, with cavities that provide shelter for fish and other organisms.Results depend on location, water conditions, species present, and the ecological goals of an individual project, but the system that began with Barber's response to a damaged Cayman reef developed into a global artificial-reef program. The foundation now lists projects involving coral transplantation, fish habitat, oyster restoration, mangroves and shoreline protection.The original motivation remained tied to what Barber had seen underwater after Hurricane Gilbert, which began as an attempt to recreate damaged reef structure and eventually became a standardized module that could be built, transported and placed underwater without the cranes and barges required for much larger artificial-reef objects.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2023, Portuguese street artist Vhils turned coal-plant remains into 13 underwater sculptures; transplanted corals now shelter octopuses, crabs and urchins
articles.summary: Rest of World News: A Portuguese street artist named Alexandre Farto, also known as Vhils, put 13 sculptures that were made from material recovered from decommissioned co.
articles.body: A Portuguese street artist named Alexandre Farto, also known as Vhils, put 13 sculptures that were made from material recovered from decommissioned coal-fired power stations beneath the Atlantic off Albufeira, Portugal. The works became the EDP Art Reef, which is an underwater exhibition designed to function as an artificial reef as marine organisms colonize the structures.Vhils' project page says the installation uses materials that were recovered from former coal plants and was commissioned by Portuguese energy company EDP. The sculptures were designed to become part of the marine environment rather than remain unchanged artworks on the seabed. The installation lies off the Algarve coast, more than 10 metres underwater and roughly a mile from shore. EDP describes the project as a combination of art, material reuse and marine-ecosystem development.From power stations to the seabedThe raw material came from three dismantled EDP thermal power stations, namely, Sines and Carregado in Portugal and Soto de Ribera in Spain. EDP said Vhils' team took three years to develop the project with the company and a group of other organizations. The 13 pieces were made from iron and concrete that had been treated for underwater use, and were divided into six groups of different shapes and sizes. Equipment that was associated with electricity generation was given a second function. Selected components became part of a permanent underwater installation instead of sending every piece of industrial material through conventional disposal or recycling routes. EDP's own account says the reef also incorporates live corals that were germinated in captivity. Researchers from the University of Algarve were expected to study and monitor the marine life developing around the structures.The sculptures were designed to changeVhils' project description says corrosion, sediment and biological growth would gradually alter the sculptures after they were submerged. Marine organisms would effectively become part of the work, and would change its appearance over time. The official EDP project page gives the installation an exhibition area of about 1,250 square metres. Eight of the 13 pieces are iron and five are concrete, and the highest structure reaches 5.3 metres, while the minimum depth of the installation is 10 metres.Divers can visit the installation, although access depends on the required diving certification and conditions at the site. The project therefore operates as an underwater art exhibition, but its physical structures also provide hard surfaces and spaces where marine organisms can attach themselves.Corals were transplanted onto the structuresPlant a Coral helped transplant coral fragments onto the structures, and TIME reported that some of the transplanted corals had been damaged by fishing nets before being moved to the new reef. The same report found that marine life had begun using the structures, including octopuses, spider crabs, urchins and fish. TIME described the installation as sitting in about 40 feet of water, which makes it accessible to divers who can reach that depth. The appearance of the sculptures has also changed underwater, since rust, sediment and biological growth cover portions of the metal and concrete.A former energy site becomes marine habitatEDP had a wider plan to move away from coal, and the company soon began decommissioning coal-fired facilities as part of its transition toward renewable energy, and material from those plants became the physical basis for the reef. EDP says the Art Reef was developed with the Centre for Marine Sciences at the University of Algarve, Portugal's maritime authorities, Albufeira City Council, Plant a Coral and other partners. Researchers were involved because the project was intended to be monitored as the marine ecosystem developed.The result is not a coral reef created entirely from transplanted coral, nor is it simply an underwater gallery, since the 13 sculptures provide the physical substrate, while corals and other marine organisms gradually occupy and alter them. Vhils' project page describes the installation as a permanent underwater exhibition and the foundation of a new artificial reef. Its appearance is expected to keep changing as corrosion, sediment and biological growth continue to work on the sculptures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'It's like layer upon layer of miracles': How Nepal flood survivors were rescued from tunnel
articles.summary: From searching for a buried tunnel entrance to blowing up rocks the size of cars, rescuers had to surmount multiple challenges to reach survivors.
articles.body:
A tunnelling expert involved in the rescue operation at a blocked Nepalese hydropower tunnel has described to the BBC how they managed to reach survivors.

Arnold Dix has been advising Nepal's hydropower authorities on how to dig through the blocked tunnel to Trishuli 3A Hydropower Station, which was one of several stations hit by last week's massive flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border.

"It's like layer upon layer of miracles" that they found two men on Friday, he said, given the multiple challenges that they faced.

The first hurdle was to locate the entrance to the tunnel, in a landscape rendered nearly unrecognisable by the flood that has so far killed 1,300 people.

"I've never known a rescue operation where you had to look for an entrance of a tunnel that was previously up the hill, that was now underground. You can imagine the enormity of the avalanche, it completely buried the entrance," said Dix, who is the president of the International Tunnelling and Underground Space Association.

Using engineering techniques, old topographic maps, satellite imagery of the area after the disaster, video footage from helicopters and "anything else we could find on the surface of the mountain such as power poles", Dix and his team triangulated the likely position of the entrance and started digging.

They found it - but the next challenge was to locate the survivors.

"We knew they would be up ahead, but we didn't know where exactly. So you just have to start digging in the right direction. And you listen out if you can hear anybody," he said.

Rescuers had to get through a tunnel blocked entirely by mud and rocks - some bigger than cars - and had to use explosives to clear the way, something they would "normally never do because of the risk of blowing up people [trapped in the tunnel] and blowing ourselves up," Dix said.

He credited the Nepalese army for doing "a wonderful job" in managing the explosions with precision to ensure they would not destabilise the tunnel.

At the same time, they discovered it was still full of water.

Using excavators and pumping machines, Nepalese rescuers dug a series of trenches from the tunnel all the way to the river outside, so they could drain the water.

Finally, they had to dig a passageway, "a tiny tunnel the size of a person", through the debris at the top of the tunnel.

The advantage of this location "is that you can use the original tunnel's roof as your little tunnel's roof. Also, it mitigates risk of flooding," Dix explained.

In the early hours of Friday morning, rescuers heard what they thought could be voices.

According to local reports, they called out "don't worry, we're here to rescue you" - and heard back a faint "okay".

Shortly after that, they pulled out Sanjaya Shah and Kabir Maharjan, alive.

But with dozens of people still thought to be trapped inside the tunnel, the work is far from over.

Dix estimated that they had dug about 60m from the entrance by now, and they would need to dig another 150m more to reach the hydropower station located deep inside the mountain.

Rescuers are hoping that the debris from the flood did not reach the station, because if it did, "there would be all kinds of complications - anybody in the station could have been hit by rocks and mud or it could be flooded".

The team on the ground are still facing significant dangers.

"Up ahead, even now, we might run into water which would drown the people tunnelling," Dix said. "And we also have the risk of another flood outside happening, so water could come from behind. So there's the risk of facing water on both ends."

But, buoyed by Friday's successful rescue, the team is now hopeful it will reach more survivors in time.

"It's a big relief, that we are on the right track. And it gives us renewed energy that our thinking [on how to conduct the rescue] works... we have never done something like this before."

Dix said they are now heading towards what he called the "Goldilocks zone" which would be "more friendly to life".

This zone is at the uppermost level of the hydropower station where there is some space where survivors may be located.

"We got two people out. If we were playing at a casino, some might say it's time to walk away, but we say game on, time to take on the house."

articles.title: Coast Guard recovers 47 bales of suspected marijuana worth $2.4M after intercepting go-fast vessel
articles.summary: The U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba intercepted a suspicious go-fast vessel and recovered 47 bales of suspected marijuana worth over $2.4 million.
articles.body: The U.S. Coast Guard recovered more than a ton of suspected marijuana worth over $2.4 million after crews intercepted a suspicious go-fast vessel during a patrol, military officials said. Crews recovered 47 bales weighing a combined 2,082 pounds along the vessel's previous route, according to Joint Interagency Task Force South (JIATF-S). Four people were detained in connection with the operation, JIATF-S said. Officials said the seizure happened during a routine patrol after the crew of U.S. Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba detected "a suspicious go-fast vessel" and launched a boat crew to investigate. NEWLY UNCLASSIFIED PENTAGON IMAGES SHOW SUSPECTED DRUG BOATS AS OFFICIAL ISSUES DEADLY WARNING "The vessel stopped without further incident," JIATF-S said. During follow-on operations, Coast Guard crews discovered what officials described as a "bale field" along the vessel's prior track and recovered the suspected marijuana, valued at more than $2.4 million. "This mission required vigilance, professionalism, and seamless coordination from detection and pursuit to evidence recovery and search-and-rescue support," JIATF-S said. WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES JIATF-S did not specify where the incident took place, but thanked the Coast Guard Cutter Escanaba and Joint Rescue Coordination Center Haiti for their "timely support, search assistance, and coordination throughout the operation." The drug seizure comes amid the Trump administration's ongoing campaign targeting narcotics trafficking networks in the Western Hemisphere. U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM) touted the operation, saying the "bust is another demonstration of the United States' resolve to stop the flow of dangerous drugs into the homeland." This week, SOUTHCOM said it conducted two operations in which U.S. forces intercepted and sank vessels in the Eastern Pacific that the military said were tied to Los Choneros, which it described as a violent narco-terrorist organization. US KILLS TWO 'NARCO-TERRORISTS' IN STRIKE 2 MONTHS SINCE LAST ANNOUNCED ANTI-'NARCO-TRAFFICKING' ATTACK The U.S. military has also been involved in a monthslong campaign launched by the Trump administration aimed at dismantling cartel-linked trafficking networks, including dozens of strikes in the Eastern Pacific and Caribbean targeting vessels it says are connected to "narco-terrorists." articles.title: From grasslands to GPUs: Why China is building its AI engine in Inner Mongolia - explained in 5 charts
articles.summary: China News: China’s artificial-intelligence boom is no longer confined to laboratories, software companies or technology districts in its biggest cities.By the en.
articles.body: China’s artificial-intelligence boom is no longer confined to laboratories, software companies or technology districts in its biggest cities.By the end of 2025, China had 602 million generative-AI users, up 141.7 per cent from a year earlier, according to the China Internet Network Information Center (CNNIC). The country’s core AI industry was valued at more than 1.2 trillion yuan in 2025, while the number of AI companies surpassed 6,200, according to China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.That surge in AI adoption is driving an equally rapid expansion in computing infrastructure. China’s intelligent computing capacity reached 1.59 million PFLOPS by the end of 2025, according to the National Data Administration. A petaflop (P) measures computing performance, with one P representing one quadrillion floating-point operations per second.But AI needs more than algorithms. It needs enormous amounts of computing power, and the electricity, cooling, land and network infrastructure required to keep that computing power running.One of the unexpected places emerging as a supplier of this infrastructure is Ulanqab, a city in Inner Mongolia better known for its grasslands, livestock and potatoes than for artificial intelligence.The transformation is striking. In 2010, Ulanqab’s economy was still firmly rooted in agriculture and animal husbandry. By 2013, the city had begun laying the foundations of a data-centre industry, with Huawei’s data-centre project marking an early milestone in its computing build-out.Over the following years, Ulanqab developed its cloud-computing base before making a sharper shift from general-purpose CPU computing to GPU-based intelligent computing in late 2022 and 2023, according to Ulanqab authorities.By August 2026, the city’s operating computing capacity had reached 172,000P, with intelligent computing accounting for more than 95 per cent, according to figures published by the Saihan District People’s Government, citing Xinhua.Computing is now becoming an increasingly important part of Ulanqab’s economic and infrastructure landscape.Livestock and farming to AI hubFive charts show how a grassland economy became one of China’s emerging computing hubs, and why scaling that transformation will require much more than simply adding servers.From farms and livestock to computing(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();Ulanqab remains very much an agricultural and livestock economy. In 2025, its agriculture, forestry, animal husbandry and fisheries sector generated ¥34.75 billion, more than double the ¥14.1 billion recorded in 2011.But alongside that established economy, a new one has been taking shape.Ulanqab’s data-centre industry began with Huawei’s arrival in 2013 and has since grown into a major computing cluster. By 2025, the city’s computing industry was generating ¥6.8 billion in annual revenue, according to Ulanqab authorities.The point is not that computing has replaced farms, livestock or potatoes. Instead, a city long associated with grasslands and animal husbandry is developing a second economic identity around something far less visible: servers, data centres and AI computing.That transformation received another major push from China’s “East Data, West Computing” strategy, which seeks to move computing infrastructure towards resource-rich western regions while connecting it to demand in the country’s densely populated east.Inner Mongolia was designated one of China’s eight national computing hub nodes, with Ulanqab’s Jining Big Data Industrial Park included in the starting area of the national hub.The result is an unusual economic mix: agricultural and livestock production continues at scale, while a growing computing industry is being built around the region’s wind, land, cooling conditions and access to renewable power.The computing base(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The next question is whether Ulanqab’s data-centre push is simply a collection of individual projects or whether it has evolved into a genuinely expanding computing cluster.The numbers point to the latter.Ulanqab’s operating computing capacity rose from 24,000P in 2024 to more than 71,000P by June 2025 and 125,000P by the end of 2025. The city says about 75,000P of its capacity is currently serving demand originating from Beijing, linking the Inner Mongolian computing cluster to one of China’s largest technology markets.Ulanqab is therefore becoming part of a wider computing network in which AI workloads can be processed in a region with abundant energy, cooler temperatures and high-speed links to major technology centres.Why put AI servers on grasslands?Ulanqab’s appeal comes down to an unusual combination of resources that AI computing consumes heavily: electricity, cooling and connectivity.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The city sits in a region rich in wind and solar power. By the end of 2025, Ulanqab’s new-energy installed capacity had exceeded 20.3GW, while green electricity accounted for 67 per cent of the city’s overall electricity use. The algorithms, companies and users may be concentrated elsewhere, but an increasingly meaningful share of the computing capacity supporting them can sit hundreds of kilometres away, on land historically associated with farming and livestock.Ulanqab’s contribution, therefore, is less about becoming an AI headquarters and more about becoming an AI infrastructure base, turning its natural resources and geography into computing capacity usable across China.Rising power bill(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();The same numbers that demonstrate Ulanqab’s success also reveal its emerging constraint.The city’s computing industry consumed 3.267 billion kWh of electricity in the first half of 2026, up 89.52 per cent from a year earlier. That implies first-half 2025 consumption of roughly 1.72 billion kWh.In other words, electricity demand almost doubled in a year.That is the catch in building an AI hub around cheap power. Once thousands of high-density GPUs arrive, cheap electricity alone is not enough. The grid must deliver power reliably, transmission and substations must keep pace, and renewable generation has to be backed by storage or other balancing capacity.Ulanqab is already responding. Its latest projects increasingly combine renewable generation, storage and dedicated power infrastructure rather than treating electricity as something that can simply be purchased from the grid.But the scale of the planned build-out remains enormous.At the end of 2025, Ulanqab had 125,000P of computing capacity. By June 2026, that had risen to 172,000P, while the city’s target for the end of 2026 is more than 200,000P.There is another limitation: talent and local value creation.Ulanqab has built training programmes and computing-related courses, but local officials themselves identify skilled digital workers as a continuing constraint. The challenge for the city is to build an ecosystem around its data centres rather than remain merely a place where servers sit.Takeaway: What India could learnUlanqab’s transformation points to a broader shift in the economics of AI. As computing demand grows, the location of servers could matter almost as much as the location of the companies building the AI.The city’s advantage does not come from any single factor. It comes from the combination of renewable power, a naturally cool climate, available land, grid infrastructure and fast connectivity to a major technology market.That combination has allowed Ulanqab to build computing infrastructure far from China’s traditional technology centres while remaining closely connected to them.The lesson for India is not to recreate Ulanqab in one particular location. It is to think of AI infrastructure as an energy-and-computing ecosystem rather than simply a collection of data centres.India’s data-centre capacity is expanding rapidly, but much of the investment remains concentrated around established technology and business centres. As AI workloads become more power-intensive, states with abundant renewable energy, reliable grids, cooler climates and available land could potentially emerge as the next generation of computing hubs.Ulanqab offers a glimpse of what that future could look like: a city once better known for livestock and potatoes becoming an important part of the infrastructure powering a national AI economy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Ed Leedskalnin spent nearly 30 years cutting and moving 1,100 tons of Florida limestone mostly alone at night; he died in 1951 without fully revealing his methods
articles.summary: US News: Discover the intriguing story of Edward Leedskalnin, the enigmatic creator of Coral Castle in Florida, who spent 28 years constructing a limestone monument alone at night and died without revealing his secrets.
articles.body: For almost three decades, Edward Leedskalnin labored on his project without many people witnessing him doing so. This was because he constructed his creation mostly at night at a place in South Florida where he moved stones weighing more than the capacity of many industrial cranes of today. At the time of his death on December 7, 1951, he had managed to erect a structure made up of limestone, which he himself never managed to explain how.Buying land in Florida City in 1923 Leedskalnin was born in Latvia on January 12, 1887, according to the ‘About Edward Leedskalnin’ page on the official Coral Castle website. He grew up in a family of average financial resources and learned stonemasonry from his own family while still in Latvia. His whole life changed when his fiancée, whom he affectionately called his "sweet sixteen," left him for another man. Heartbroken, he left Europe, immigrated to the United States, and eventually settled in Florida after being diagnosed with tuberculosis. There, he bought a small piece of land for around $10-$12 and began what became his lifelong project: a monument made entirely out of stone in memory of the woman who had left him.Nearly three decades of solitary constructionWorking alone and almost always at night, Leedskalnin quarried and shaped about 1,100 tons of local oolitic limestone, a porous rock formed from ancient coral and shells that is considerably lighter than it looks. He relied on nothing more advanced than winches, pulleys and tools he built himself from salvaged car parts, a construction method described in an entry from the Encyclopaedia Britannica. One of his inventions was a nine-ton stone door pivoted on an iron pin and counterbalanced with ball bearings, so that it could be opened with just one finger. Leedskalnin himself stood barely five feet tall and weighed about 120 pounds; there was no clear explanation for how a person of his stature was able to lift such massive blocks.Relocating the entire structure in 1936In 1936, Leedskalnin found out that there was a plan for a housing complex near his land in Florida City and to avoid any loss of privacy, he chose to relocate his entire structure. He bought a ten-acre plot of land about ten miles away in Homestead, where he relocated his complete stone carvings one by one, a process that is said to have taken two to three years, as per Visit Florida.He also did his moving work only at night, when he filled the gaps in his walls with smaller rocks so that no one would be able to see through them during the day. He managed to move the stones with a truck chassis fitted with rails, towed by his friend's tractor. It is estimated that one of the stones being moved was between 29 and 30 tons.A method he took to his graveVisits to Leedskalnin's land were charged 10 cents per person, but he later increased it to 25 cents. As visitors entered his land, the stone sign at the entrance read: ‘You will be seeing unusual accomplishment’. When people would ask him how he constructed such an elaborate castle, all he could give away was the use of physics, levers and the "secrets" of construction in ancient buildings such as the Pyramids. He died on December 7, 1951, at the age of 64, from pneumonia. He spent almost thirty years building what he built largely on his own, using construction methods he never wrote down or demonstrated to anyone else.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: JONATHAN TURLEY: Talarico brings a touch of Trotsky to the Texas Senate race
articles.summary: Video shows James Talarico at a climate forum calling capitalism an "oppressive system" linked to White supremacy that must be "dismantled."
articles.body: Senate Democratic nominee James Talarico appears ready to bring a touch of Trotsky to Texas. In a video from a climate forum, Talarico is shown declaring capitalism an "oppressive system" linked with White supremacy and saying that it must be "dismantled" to achieve a better world. It is reminiscent of Russian revolutionary Leon Trotsky, who denounced the "fundamental evil of the capitalist system" and called on citizens to free themselves from its oppression. The Democratic Socialists of America and radical sites have long called "to dismantle the capitalist state." As a state representative, Talarico addressed the 2020 climate conference by the Austin chapter of the Sierra Club with other Texas House candidates. However, it was Talarico who roused the crowd with an attack on capitalism: "I’m so thankful that you asked this question and also thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country ... And I think only ending the ways that all three of those oppressive systems work together are we gonna be able to begin the process of dismantling them." TALARICO’S ‘PROUD CAPITALIST’ ABOUT-FACE COLLIDES WITH RESURFACED CALL TO ‘DISMANTLE’ CAPITALISM Talarico added criticism of Texas’s oil and gas industry, which he mocked as a dying industry "like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s." He predicted with obvious satisfaction, "That industry is not gonna last." Ironically, given his earlier promise of running a meatless, vegan campaign, opposing both beef and energy markets in Texas could well achieve the dismantling of the economy by default in Texas. WATCH: UNEARTHED VIDEO SHOWS LEFTIST SENATE HOPEFUL CELEBRATING ANTI-FOSSIL FUEL GROUP'S ARRIVAL IN TEXAS Talarico's views closely parallel socialist and communist talking points online. The Democratic Socialists of America has challenged people to "imagine the end of capitalism." Those words in The Democratic Socialists of America manifesto offer Americans a world without landlords, debt, mandatory work hours, and "food, education, energy, medicine, and transportation … are common goods and utilities." The DSA is premised on the same stated objective of Talarico, declaring that there has to be "a revolutionary transformation to replace the capitalist social order based on exploitation and oppression." JONATHAN TURLEY: DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS WANT TO REMAKE AMERICA IN THEIR IMAGE. THAT’S TERRIFYING Other candidates have sought to pander to this radical mob. Recently, California Democrat Gov. Gavin Newsom thrilled the mob by declaring that "nostalgia is not working," adding that "capitalism as we know it doesn’t work either." In "Rage and the Republic," I discuss the rise of socialism and the coalition of politicians, pundits and professors in attacking capitalism as well as core institutions such as the Supreme Court. It is a crisis of faith on the 250th anniversary of the oldest and most successful republic in history. SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM It is the 250th anniversary not only of the Declaration of Independence but of Adam Smith’s "Wealth of Nations." Smith's free-market theories were immediately embraced by the Founders as the perfect economic theory to match their political theory. They had declared the first Enlightenment Revolution based on a belief in natural rights that came from God, not governments. However, those rights mean little without economic freedom. Capitalism offered citizens the ability to transcend class and social barriers, to advance as far as their skills and labor would take them. MODERN CAPITALISM IS TURNING 250, TOO. WE NEED TO REMIND AMERICANS WHY IT’S IMPORTANT Together, those political and economic theories created the most prosperous and stable democratic system in the world. That system is now under attack on both sides. Radicals are calling for the trashing of the U.S. Constitution and the discarding of our core constitutional values. The DSA is premised on the same stated objective of Talarico, declaring that there has to be "a revolutionary transformation to replace the capitalist social order based on exploitation and oppression." Even establishment figures from former Vice President Kamala Harris to Newsom now dismiss faith in core institutions as mere "nostalgia." Those of us who support the Madisonian democracy are derisively called "institutionalists" and constitutional "cultists." JONATHAN TURLEY: DEM SOCIALIST RIPS ‘INSTITUTIONALISTS’ AS FAR LEFT TURNS UP HEAT ON DEFENDERS OF CONSTITUTION The New York Times ran a column, "The Constitution Is Broken and Should Not Be Reclaimed," by Ryan D. Doerfler of Harvard and Samuel Moyn of Yale, calling upon citizens to "reclaim America from constitutionalism." As these attacks on our constitutional system mount, a similar attack on capitalism is unfolding. In New York, Democratic Mayor Zohran Mamdani promised to show citizens the "warmth of collectivism" from free childcare to free buses to state-run grocery stores. Across the country, Mamdani allies are joining him in calling for the de-commodification of private property and the seizing of the means of production. DSA CO-CHAIR MOCKED FOR PROUDLY CONFIRMING SOCIALISTS WANT TO ABOLISH THE SENATE, NATIONAL BORDERS, PRISONS Polls show that these candidates are being propelled not by the working class, but by young, college-educated voters fresh out of the ideological echo chamber of higher education. They are armchair revolutionaries like Talarico, repeating socialist slogans with the same robotic rote delivery of a Young Pioneer camp. As these videos surface, radical candidates from Michigan Democrat Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to Talarico brush off their earlier comments as media allies attack any reporting on prior statements. New York Democrat Socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, who is considering a run for president, recently called her own extremist statements "Woke 1." SOCIALIST CANDIDATES CAN DELETE OLD POSTS, BUT THEY CAN'T ERASE THEIR RADICALISM The transparent insincerity does not matter to their base. These figures have already shown their bona fides with extremist statements in the past. Talarico's desire to dismantle capitalism was not some slip of the tongue but a planned speech to fellow activists. To pivot now is considered to be mere packaging for uneducated and malleable dupes. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Indeed, the Talarico campaign responded by simply declaring that Talarico is a "proud capitalist," though one staffer admitted that the comments were a bit "cringey." Being a "proud capitalist" who wants to "dismantle" capitalism is a bit like being an avid meat-eater who denounces meat consumption as killing the world and banning meat from his campaign." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Accordingly, when asked about past radical positions, these figures immediately deny or dismiss them. If you want to dismantle the constitutional or economic systems of the United States, a few white lies hardly seem of much consequence. After all, as Trotsky explained, "The end may justify the means as long as there is something that justifies the end." For these radicals, there is no greater justification than their own election. articles.title: ‘No inconvenience to devotees’: CM Yogi Adityanath pitches grand temple complexes in Mathura-Vrindavan
articles.summary: MATHURA: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday said the state government plans to develop grand temple complexes in Mathura-Vrindavan.
articles.body: MATHURA: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Friday said the state government plans to develop grand temple complexes in Mathura-Vrindavan on the lines of those in Ayodhya and Kashi.The statement by the chief minister came on the second day of his visit to Mathura. He arrived at the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi Temple on Friday morning on the occasion of Shri Krishna Janmashtami.The chief minister first performed ritual worship of cows in the Shri Krishna Janmabhoomi complex. Following the gau pujan, Adityanath offered special prayers and sought blessings from ‘Lala’ (Lord Krishna), who is enshrined in the main sanctum sanctorum.After offering prayers in the main sanctum, Adityanath also visited the Yogmaya Temple, Keshavdev Temple and Bhagwat Bhavan, located within the complex.Speaking to the press after his visit, the CM said, "Today, you will not even be able to find invaders. They have all disappeared. A grand temple of Lord Ram has been built in Ayodhya. One of the world’s largest temples has come up in Ayodhya. Those who do not like all this are trying to defame Ayodhya. After a wait of 500 years, that work has finally been accomplished... Keeping in mind the spiritual and cultural significance of this Braj region, the Braj Teerth Vikas Parishad, along with public representatives, is working to develop it in a manner befitting its importance and to provide better facilities for devotees. Our effort is to create a similar devotee-friendly environment and infrastructure in Mathura and Vrindavan as has been developed in Ayodhya and Kashi, so that no devotee faces any inconvenience and there is no obstacle or threat to their faith."Taking a swipe at political opponents, Adityanath said his government believed in “Krishna Kanhaiya, Lord Ram, Baba Vishwanath and Maa Vindhyavasini” and respected the faith of the people.“But can those whose faith lies in Babur and Aurangzeb respect your faith?” he asked, accusing the “followers of Babur and Aurangzeb” of attempting to create divisions in society.Adityanath alleged that such forces wanted to weaken social harmony, compromise security, play with the future of young people and threaten the safety of women. He said the BJP’s “double-engine government” would not allow such designs to succeed.The chief minister also contrasted the present government’s approach with that of previous administrations, claiming that earlier governments avoided visiting such places because of “vote-bank concerns”.Referring to the changing identity of the Braj region, Adityanath said it was now being associated with religious and cultural celebrations, including Rangotsav, Braj Raj Utsav and Vaishnav Kumbh, rather than incidents of violence and disorder.Extending Janmashtami greetings to people across Uttar Pradesh, Adityanath called upon citizens to remain committed to their duties towards the country, society, Sanatan Dharma and their families.“If everyone fulfils their responsibilities honestly, it will not take long for India to become a developed nation and Uttar Pradesh a developed state,” he said.Notably, this is not the first time that the CM has spoken about developing temple complexes in Mathura on the lines of those in Ayodhya and Varanasi. He has repeatedly linked Mathura-Vrindavan’s religious development with the transformation of Ayodhya and Kashi, including in 2021-22 when he spoke about Mathura and Vrindavan after the Ram Temple and Kashi Vishwanath projects."There were numerous invasions, and many attempted to impose their own faiths upon India, yet no one could erase Sanatan Dharma. Those who had the audacity to try and obliterate Sanatan Dharma were themselves reduced to dust and faded into oblivion. However, not only in Braj Bhoomi but across all of India, the memory of Shri Krishna and Radha Rani serves as an inspiration for us today and fosters an atmosphere of enthusiasm and progress for future generations," Yogi Adityanath said.Janmashtami, also known as Krishna Janmashtami or Gokulashtami, is observed to mark the birth of Lord Krishna, regarded as the eighth avatar of Lord Vishnu.The festival is observed on the eighth day, or Ashtami, of the Krishna Paksha in the month of Bhadrapada, according to the Hindu lunisolar calendar.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Lucknow | Silver Rate in Lucknow | Bank Holidays in Lucknow | Public Holidays in Lucknow | Lucknow AQI | Weather in Lucknow | Petrol Price in Lucknow | Diesel Price in Lucknow | CNG Price in Lucknow | LPG Price in LucknowStay updated with the latest Lucknow news.
